title: Visibilising the gritty realities of truck driving work in the UK
affiliations: Department for Continuing Education, University of Oxford, UK
abstract: This article introduces Josephine (Jo) Noon, a woman truck driver in her early 40s. Speaking as a woman in a male-dominated occupation, a recent entrant into the UK’s truck driving workforce and with experience driving in the UK and Europe, Jo’s account disrupts common misconceptions about truck driving and truck drivers. The article contributes to sociological debates at the intersections of mobility and labour by drawing attention to how spatial mobility itself constitutes work for mobile logistics workers and becomes a site of surplus extraction for capital. We highlight the less explored material, embodied realities of occupational auto-mobilities, and the physical infrastructures necessary for the daily social reproduction of mobile workers, foregrounding their affective, generative effects for worker wellbeing and retention. The article ends with a provocation: that truck driver shortages be read as a ‘refusal’ by drivers to continue labouring under exploitative logistics capital and uncaring state actors.

title: Authenticity of scientific literature: analyzing the usage of hedging in adapted scientific literature
abstract: Abstract Adapted scientific literature (ASL) is increasingly used in educational contexts to make authentic science texts accessible to students. One hallmark of scientific writing is the use of hedging - linguistic means to express uncertainty or tentativeness. This study investigates whether ASL maintains this characteristic feature, and to what extent its usage of hedging aligns with original scientific articles. Using a machine learning approach, we trained classifiers on the BioScope corpus to automatically detect hedging in English and German texts. We then analyzed corpora consisting of original research articles, their adapted counterparts, and textbook excerpts. Our results show that ASL retains the typical distributional pattern of hedging - particularly its increased frequency in the introduction and discussion sections - but the overall proportion of hedging expressions is reduced compared to the original texts. In contrast, textbook texts contain very little hedging and present scientific knowledge as more certain. These findings suggest that ASL offers a linguistically authentic alternative to original scientific literature and may help learners engage with the epistemic practices of science more realistically. While some reduction in hedging occurs during the adaptation process, ASL preserves essential rhetorical features of scientific discourse and can thus serve as a valuable resource in science education.

title: The Role of Public Administrators in Building a Robust Liberal Democracy
affiliations: Department of Social Sciences and Business Roskilde University Roskilde Denmark
abstract: ABSTRACT After decades of expansion, liberal democracy is threatened by autocratic populists. These actors exploit widening gaps between leaders and citizens, as well as growing political polarization in the population, to consolidate executive power by undermining courts, sidelining elected assemblies, discrediting public administrators, and intimidating both opposition and the press. This alarming predicament begs the question of what enterprising role public administrators can play in curbing the rise of autocratic populism by reconnecting elected politicians with diverse and polarized population groups while fostering alignment among them. To this end, public administrators are conceptualized as bridgebuilders promoting interactive political leadership along the vertical axis of the political system; as mediators fostering agreement, accommodation, or compromise between polarized groups along the horizontal axis; and as institutional architects linking representative democracy and collaborative governance arenas. This expanded role of public administrators as democratic guardians and protagonists raises important questions regarding its legitimacy.

title: Increasing Equitable Access in Public Service: A Descriptive Study About Accessible Materials
affiliations: School of Politics, Public Affairs, and International Studies, University of Wyoming Laramie Wyoming USA
abstract: ABSTRACT As the digital footprint of public service expands, the need for accessible materials for individuals with disabilities grows. Public servants must consider accessibility in the creation of all materials, from websites to PDFs to audio and visual media. However, research around accessible material creation in public service has been limited. This study uses data from a 2024 survey of MPA alumni from five universities to identify their familiarity with accessible material creation, including their awareness of their own organization's policies, processes, and training. The findings reveal that respondent awareness of their own organization's practices was correlated with higher familiarity in generating accessible materials. However, many respondents did not know about their organization's practices, identifying the need for increased dialogue about this essential element of social equity and inclusion. As such, suggestions for organizations to improve their practices around accessible material creation along with ideas for continued research are shared.

title: Maximizing the Out-of-Sample Sharpe Ratio
affiliations: Louvain Finance, Louvain Institute of Data Analysis and Modeling, UCLouvain, 1348 Louvain-la-Neuve, Belgium
abstract: Analytical Approach to Sharpe Ratio Optimization Under Estimation Risk In “Maximizing the Out-of-Sample Sharpe Ratio,” the author studies how investors can optimize their out-of-sample Sharpe ratio when the mean vector and covariance matrix of asset returns are estimated from limited historical data. The author derives analytical expressions for the expectation and variance of the out-of-sample Sharpe ratio for portfolio rules located on the sample mean-variance efficient frontier. With these results at hand, the author identifies the optimal location on the efficient frontier in the presence of estimation risk. The author provides simulation and empirical evidence demonstrating the benefits of the proposed portfolio rules relative to several benchmarks. This paper extends the mathematical toolkit for portfolio selection under parameter uncertainty by addressing the challenge of optimizing the out-of-sample Sharpe ratio in a nonasymptotic setting.

title: The Impact of Gender Information on Hiring Decisions Based on Self-Set Performance Targets
authors: Katharina Werner; Susanna Grundmann; Bettina Rockenbach
affiliations: Department of Economics, Faculty of Management, Economics and Social Sciences, University of Cologne, D-50923 Cologne, Germany; and Department of Economics and Finance, OMNES Education, International University of Monaco, OMNES Education, 98000 Principality of Monaco, Monaco; Department of Economics, Faculty of Management, Economics and Social Sciences, University of Cologne, D-50923 Cologne, Germany
abstract: Gender-anonymous hiring practices have been widely advocated as a means to reduce labor market inequalities, such as the gender wage gap and the underrepresentation of women in leadership. However, their effectiveness remains debated. This paper studies an experimental labor market where employee candidates set their own performance targets for a real-effort task and employers hire based on these self-set targets. In many professional settings, such targets serve as performance indicators and influence hiring and promotion decisions. In an online experiment with 4,674 participants, we vary in a 2 × 2 design (1) whether employers know the candidates’ genders and (2) the severity of the payoff consequences if the hired employee misses their target. This allows us to examine the interaction effects of gender anonymity in hiring and the performance target’s payoff relevance. We find that given equal ability, women set lower targets than men. Higher targets increase the likelihood of being hired, whereas a larger expected target-performance gap reduces hiring chances, particularly when missing the target has severe consequences for the employer. Importantly, our findings suggest that gender-anonymous applications may have unintended consequences. When gender is revealed, employers appear to adjust for gender differences in target setting, expecting a smaller target-performance gap for women than for men. As a result, women are more likely to be hired and receive higher payoffs when their gender is known. These results indicate that gender-anonymous hiring may backfire for women by preventing employers from accounting for behavioral gender differences (e.g., in self-promotion), ultimately reducing women’s hiring prospects. This paper was accepted by Dorothea Kübler, behavioral economics and decision analysis. title: Group-Sparse Matrix Factorization for Transfer Learning of Word Embeddings
authors: Kan Xu; Xuanyi Zhao; Hamsa Bastani; Osbert Bastani
affiliations: W. P. Carey School of Business, Arizona State University, Tempe, Arizona 85281; University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania 19104; Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania 19104
abstract: Unstructured text provides decision makers with a rich data source in many domains, ranging from product reviews in retail to nursing notes in healthcare. To leverage this information, words are typically translated into word embeddings—vectors that encode the semantic relationships between words—through unsupervised learning algorithms such as matrix factorization. However, learning word embeddings from new domains with limited training data can be challenging because the meaning/usage may be different in the new domain; for example, the word “positive” typically has positive sentiment, but often has negative sentiment in medical notes because it may imply that a patient tested positive for a disease. In practice, we expect that only a small number of domain-specific words may have new meanings. We propose an intuitive two-stage estimator that exploits this structure via a group-sparse penalty to efficiently transfer learn domain-specific word embeddings by combining large-scale text corpora (such as Wikipedia) with limited domain-specific text data. We bound the generalization error of our transfer learning estimator, proving that it can achieve high accuracy with substantially less domain-specific data when only a small number of embeddings are altered between domains. Furthermore, we prove that all local minima identified by our nonconvex objective function are statistically indistinguishable from the global minimum under standard regularization conditions, implying that our estimator can be computed efficiently. Our results provide the first bounds on group-sparse matrix factorization, which may be of independent interest. We empirically evaluate our approach compared with state-of-the-art fine-tuning heuristics from natural language processing. This paper was accepted by Chung Piaw Teo, optimization. title: Inflation in Reputation Systems? Newcomers, Veterans, and Socialization within a Platform Community
authors: Mareike Möhlmann; Nicholas Berente; Yoonseock Son; John Lalor
affiliations: Bentley University, Information and Process Management, Waltham, Massachusetts, 02452-4705, United States; University of Notre Dame, Mendoza College of Business, Notre Dame, United States; University of Notre Dame, IT, Analytics, and Operations, Notre Dame, Indiana, 46556, United States; University of Notre Dame Mendoza College of Business, IT, Analytics, and Operations, Notre Dame, Indiana, 46556-5646, United States
abstract: Rating inflation is prevalent in reputation systems and can reduce their informational value. Through an exploratory mixed‐method study, we examine how and why rating inflation behavior evolves over time as reviewers socialize within an online reputation system platform community. We show that some reviewers are more prone to inflation while others avoid it. We draw on the theory of reciprocity and distinguish among three archetypical phases of reviewers: (1) the Newcomer Phase, (2) the Inflator Phase, and (3) the Veteran Phase. Newcomers who are not yet socialized in the platform community are less likely to inflate their ratings. Inflators exhibit the social norm of direct reviewer reciprocity and inflate their ratings. Veterans, reflecting the social norm of generalized reviewer reciprocity, are less likely to inflate ratings. Instead, they are more candid because they are driven by a commitment to help the platform community. These archetypical phases correspond to reviewers’ increasing socialization within the platform community and exposure to different digital platform affordances. Together, these processes shape which forms of reciprocity become salient over time—whether lacking, direct, or generalized—which consequently drive distinct reviewer behaviors. While most research on rating inflation emphasizes direct reciprocity, we highlight how reviewers can shift toward less inflated behaviors over time, aligning with generalized reciprocity towards the platform community. Thus, this exploratory work suggests an evolutionary process of rating behavior whereby rating inflation follows an inverted U-shape over the reviewer lifecycle.

abstract: Gerard Roland of University of California, Berkeley and CEPR reviews “Globalisation, Development and Transition: Conversations with Eminent Economists” by Brian Snowdon,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Provides a comprehensive survey of the major economic issues that have helped shape the modern world. Discusses the fall and rise of globalization; economic development in historical perspective; and the rise and fall of the socialist system and the trials of transition. Includes interviews with eleven leading economists. Snowdon is Professor of Economics and International Business in the Newcastle Business School at Northumbria University. Bibliography; index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Anne O. Krueger of Johns Hopkins University reviews “Fixing Global Finance” by Martin Wolf,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Analyzes the weaknesses of the global financial system of the early twenty-first century and considers possibilities for a different international financial architecture. Discusses learning lessons; blessings and perils of global finance; the move from crises to imbalances; the calm before a storm; the move toward adjustment and domestic reform; the move toward global reform; and the move toward a more stable world. Wolf is Professor of Economics at the University of Nottingham. Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: John Diamond of Rice University reviews “Tax Policy and Labor Market Performance” by Jonas Agell, Peter Birch Sorensen,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Eight papers, originally presented at the CESifo Summer Institute held in July 2003 in Venice, analyze the effect of tax policy and welfare state incentives on the performance of the labor market. Papers discuss tax policy and labor market performance (A. Lans Bovenberg); work and taxes (Stephen Nickell); whether social policies harm employment and growth--second-best effects of taxes and benefits on employment (Frederick van der Ploeg); welfare effects of tax reform and labor supply at the intensive and extensive margins (Nada Eissa, Henrik Jacobsen Kleven, and Claus Thustrup Kreiner); the hours of work response of married couples--taxes and the earned income credit (‘Eissa and Hilary Hoynes); progressive taxation and wages--microevidence (Torben Tranas, Soren Arnberg, and Anders Holm); insiders, outsiders, and the underground economy (Dan Anderberg); and wages, unemployment, and the underground economy (Ann-Sofie Kolm and Birthe Larsen). Agell is Professor of Economics at Stockholm University. Sorensen is Professor of Macroeconomic Theory and Policy at the University of Copenhagen. Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: John Diamond of Rice University reviews “Taxing Corporate Income in the 21st Century” by Alan J. Auerbach, James R. Hines, Joel Slemrod,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Nine papers and eighteen comments, originally presented at a conference held at the Stephen M. Ross School of Business at the University of Michigan in May 2005, explore issues surrounding the corporation income tax. Papers discuss the effects of taxes on market responses to dividend announcements and payments--what we can learn from the 2003 dividend tax cut; dissecting dividend decisions--some clues about the effects of dividend taxation from recent U.K. reforms; the 2003 dividend tax cuts and the value of the firm--an event study; how elastic the corporate income tax base is; an empirical examination of corporate tax noncompliance; the extent, growth, and efficiency consequences of state business tax planning; corporate taxation and international competition; the changing role of auditors in corporate tax planning; and taxation and the evolution of aggregate corporate ownership concentration. Auerbach is Robert D. Burch Professor of Economics and Law and Director of the Burch Center for Tax Policy and Public Finance at the University of California, Berkeley. Hines is Richard A. Musgrave Collegiate Professor of Economics and Professor of Law at the University of Michigan. Slemrod is Paul W. McCracken Collegiate Professor of Business Economics and Public Policy at the University of Michigan. Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: John Diamond of Rice University reviews “Reining in the Competition for Capital” by Ann Markusen,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Eight papers, originally presented at a conference hosted by the University of Minnesota’s Humphrey Institute of Public Affairs in the spring of 2004, explore the causes, character, and potential remedies for the growing spatial competition for capital. Papers discuss institutional and political determinants of incentive competition (Ann Markusen and Katherine Nesse); the sources and processes of tax and subsidy competition (Kenneth P. Thomas); the fiscal consequences of competition for capital (Peter Fisher); how the European Union manages subsidy competition (Adinda Sinnaeve); solving the problems of economic development incentives (Timothy J. Bartik); negotiating the ideal deal--which local governments have the most bargaining leverage (Rachel Weber); whether better job creation subsidies hold real promise for business incentive reformers (William Schweke); and nine concrete ways to curtail the economic war among the states (Greg LeRoy). Markusen is a professor in the Urban and Regional Planning Graduate Program and Director of the Project on Regional and Industrial Economics at the Humphrey Institute of Public Affairs, University of Minnesota. Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Firouz Gahvari of University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign reviews “International Perspectives on Social Security Reform” by Rudolph G. Penner,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Six papers and twelve comments, originally presented at an Urban Institute conference held in February 2006, examine social security reform in six OECD countries. Papers discuss Canada (Real Bouchard); Sweden (Agneta Kruse and Edward Palmer); Japan (Tetsuo Kabe); Germany (Michael Mersmann); the United Kingdom (Alex Beer); and Italy (Alicia Puente Cackley, Tom Moscovitch, and Benjamin Pfeiffer). Penner is Senior Fellow and holds the Arjay and Frances Miller Chair in Public policy at the Urban Institute. Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Jill Horwitz of University of Michigan reviews “Reforming Medicare: Options, Tradeoffs, and Opportunities” by Henry J. Aaron,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Presents a guide to the debate over medicare reform in the United States. Discusses Medicare reform--the stakes; a Medicare primer; goals, performance, and options for Medicare; strengthening Medicare as a social insurance program; premium support; consumer-directed Medicare; and assessing Medicare reform options and prospects. Aaron is Senior Fellow in Economic Studies and Bruce and Virginia MacLaury Chair at the Brookings Institution. Lambrew is Associate Professor in the Lyndon B. Johnson School of Public Affairs at the University of Texas AT Austin, and Senior Fellow at the Center for American Progress. Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Ed Hopkins of University of Edinburgh reviews “Happiness: A Revolution in Economics” by Bruno S. Frey,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Explores the major developments of happiness research in economics and considers the new insights we have gained into how income, unemployment, inflation, and income demonstration affect well-being. Discusses research on happiness; the relationship of happiness to utility; how income affects happiness; how unemployment affects happiness; how inflation and inequality affect happiness; the public sphere; self-employment and voluntary work; marriage and happiness; watching television; procedural utility; mispredicting utility; the value of public goods; happiness policies; happiness and political institutions; and a revolution in economics. Frey is Professor of Economics at the University of Zurich and Research Director of the Center for Research in Economics, Management, and the Arts. Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Gary Burtless of The Brookings Institution reviews “The Competition of Ideas: The World of the Washington Think Tanks” by Murray Weidenbaum, Jeanne M. Lambrew,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Examines the political economy of the Washington, D.C. think tanks. Discusses the challenge facing think tanks; basic data on Washington think tanks; the five major think tanks; making some comparisons; how think tanks operate; think tanks and business; and measuring the influence of think tanks. Weidenbaum is Edward Mallinckrodt Distinguished University Professor of Economics at Washington University in St. Louis. Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Nicholas Barr of London School of Economics and Political Science reviews “When I’m Sixty-Four: The Plot against Pensions and the Plan to Save Them” by Teresa Ghilarducci,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Examines the looming retirement crisis for baby boomers and others who hope to retire in the coming years, and considers a plan to guarantee retirement security for every working citizen. Discusses hope for retirement’s future; the collapse of retirement income; when bad things happen to good pensions--when promises get broken; do-it-yourself pensions; the future of social security; the short history of old age leisure in America; the distribution of retirement time--who really gets to retire; working--the new retirement’s effect on the economy; the American labor movement--advocating retirement and obtaining pensions; and a rescue plan for American workers’ retirement--averting the end of retirement. Ghilarducci is Irene and Bernard L. Schwartz Chair of Economic Policy Analysis at the New School for Social Research, and Wurf Fellow at Harvard University School of Law. Glossary; bibliography; index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Lawrence R. Glosten of Columbia University reviews “Information and Learning in Markets: The Impact of Market Microstructure” by Xavier Vives,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Graduate-level textbook analyzes how markets aggregate information and examines the impacts of specific market arrangements on the aggregation process and overall performance of financial markets. Discusses aggregation of information in simple market mechanisms--large markets; aggregation of information in simple market mechanisms--how large is large; rational expectations and supply function competition; rational expectations and market microstructure in financial markets; strategic traders in financial markets; learning from others and herding; dynamic information aggregation; dynamic rational expectations models in competitive financial markets; and price and information dynamics in financial markets. Includes end-of-chapter exercises. Vives is Professor of Economics and Finance at the IESE Business School at the University of Navarra. Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Mirjam van Praag of University of Amsterdam reviews “Race and Entrepreneurial Success: Black-, Asian-, and White-Owned Businesses in the United States” by Robert W. Fairlie, Alicia M. Robb,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Examines racial disparities in business performance in the United States. Discusses racial disparities in business ownership and outcomes; the determinants of small business success; why African American-owned businesses are less successful; and why Asian-owned businesses are more successful. Fairlie is Professor of Economics at the University of California, Santa Cruz. Robb is Research Associate in Economics at the University of California, Santa Cruz and Senior Economist with Beacon Economics. Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Miki Seko of Keio University reviews “Accelerating Japan’s Economic Growth: Resolving Japan’s Growth Controversy” by F. Gerard Adams, Lawrence R. Klein, Yuzo Kumasaka, Akihiko Shinozaki,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Explores the impact of the information technology (IT) revolution on the Japanese production function using an econometric model of Japan and simulation studies based on a theoretical framework. Discusses the economic growth record in Japan; the challenges to Japanese economic growth; the IT/e-business revolution and globalization--implications of the New Economy for Japan; IT and productivity growth--a theoretical and empirical framework; the East Asian growth process and IT--implications for Japan; information and communications technology and productivity growth in Japan; revisiting Japanese industrial organization and the corporate system; a case study of government policy and the telecommunications market in Japan; IT-related development and policy--some examples from the United States with relevance to Japan; estimating a new economy production function for Japan; simulation studies for accelerating Japanese economic growth; policies to achieve faster economic growth in Japan; and accelerating Japan’s economic growth. Adams is Professor Emeritus at the University of Pennsylvania. Klein is a Nobel Laureate and Benjamin Franklin Professor Emeritus at the University of Pennsylvania. Kumasaka is CEO of IT Economy Advisers. Shinozaki is a professor at Kyushu University. Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Jessica Goldberg of University of Michigan reviews “Youth in Africa’s Labor Market” by Marito Garcia, Jean Fares,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Eleven papers examine the challenges African youth face in their transition to work and present a strategy for meeting these challenges. Papers discuss why it is important for Africa to invest in its youth (Marito Garcia and Jean Fares); transitions to working life for Africa’s youth (Garcia and Fares); how Africa’s young people spend their time (Garcia and Fares); the effect of education on income and employment (Garcia and Fares); working in bad jobs or not working at all (Garcia and Fares); the three pillars of policy--lessons from international experience (Garcia and Fares); school-to-work transitions--a regional overview (Lorenzo Guarcello, Marco Manacorda, Furio Rosati, Fares, Scott Lyon, and Cristina Valdivia); what determines labor market participation by youth in Burkina Faso (Daniel Parent); child labor and youth employment in Ethiopia (Guarcello, Lyon, and Rosati); youth in the labor market and the transition from school to work in Tanzania (Florence Kondylis and Manacorda); and how universal primary education affected returns to education and labor market participation in Uganda (Lisa Dragoset and Lars Vilhuber). Garcia is Lead Economist with the World Bank’s Human Development Department, Africa Region. Fares is Senior Economist with the World Bank’s Human Development Network. Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Petra Moser of Stanford University and NBER reviews “Financing Innovation in the United States, 1870 to the Present” by Naomi R. Lamoreaux, Kenneth L. Sokoloff,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Eleven papers examine the ways in which innovation has been funded in the United States at different stages of economic development, beginning with the post-Civil War period of the Second Industrial Revolution. Papers discuss financing invention during the Second Industrial Revolution--Cleveland, Ohio, 1870-1920; the organizing and financing of innovative companies in the evolution of the U.S. automobile industry; why finance capitalism and the Second Industrial Revolution arose in the 1890s; funding new industries--a historical perspective on the financing role of the U.S. stock market in the twentieth century; stock market swings and the value of innovation, 1908-29; financing fiber--Corning’s invasion of the telecommunications market; the federal role in financing major innovations--information technology during the postwar period; learning the hard way--IBM and the sources of innovation in early computing; trading knowledge--an exploration of patent protection and other determinants of market transactions in technology and research and development; the governance of new firms--a functional perspective; and real effects of knowledge capital on going public and market valuation. Lamoreaux is Professor in the Departments of Economics and History at the University of California, Los Angeles. Sokoloff is Professor of Economics at the University of California, Los Angeles, and Vice President of the Economic… Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: John P. Bonin of Wesleyan University reviews “From Socialism to Capitalism: Eight Essays” by Janos Kornai,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Presents comparisons of socialism and capitalism, and dictatorship and democracy, with an interpretation of the “change of system.” Discusses the coherence of the classical system; the inner contradictions of reform socialism; market socialism or socialist market economy; the speed of transformation; the great transformation of Central Eastern Europe--success and disappointment; what “change of system” means; what countries embarking on postsocialist transformation can learn from the experiences so far; and the system paradigm. Kornai is Professor Emeritus at Harvard University, Permanent Fellow Emeritus of Collegium Budapest, Institute for Advanced Study, and Distinguished Research Professor at Central European University. Name and subject indexes.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Matthew J. Hoffmann of University of Toronto reviews “Global Warming: Looking Beyond Kyoto” by Ernesto Zedillo,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Fourteen papers, resulting from a conference hosted by the Yale Center for the Study of Globalization in October 2005, examine the economic, social, and political context of climate policy in both industrialized and developing nations, and consider a multilateral approach that goes beyond the mitigation-focused Kyoto policies. Papers discuss the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change--establishing the evidence; whether the global warming alarm is founded on fact; anthropogenic climate change--revisiting the facts; “dangerous” climate change--key vulnerabilities; the policy implications of climate change impacts; economic analyses of the Kyoto Protocol--whether there is life after Kyoto; the European Emissions Trading Regime and the future of Kyoto; climate change--designing an effective response; an international policy architecture for the post-Kyoto era; controversies of Russian climate policy and opportunities for greenhouse gas reduction; climate policy in the United Kingdom; Canada’s approach to tackling climate change; India and climate change--mitigation, adaptation, and a way forward; and correct choices for China--energy conservation, a cyclic economy, and a conservation-minded society. Zedillo is Director of the Yale Center for the Study of Globalization and Professor in the field of international economics and politics at Yale University. Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Neil De Marchi of Duke University reviews “The Patron’s Payoff: Conspicuous Commissions in Italian Renaissance Art” by Jonathan K. Nelson, Richard J. Zeckhauser,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Presents an application of the methods of information economics to the study of art. Provides overviews of the main players--patrons, artists, and audiences; the analytic framework--benefits, costs, and constraints; theories of distinction--magnificence and signaling; and selecting and magnifying information--signposting and stretching. Includes five papers that discuss private chapels in Florence--a paradise for signalers (Jonathan K. Nelson and Richard J. Zeckhauser); commissioning familial remembrance in fourteenth-century Florence--signaling Alberti patronage at the Church of Santa Croce (Thomas J. Loughman); signs of success--Leone Leoni’s signposting in sixteenth-century Milan (Kelley Helmstutler Di Dio); Andrea Mantegna’s Madonna della Vittoria and the rewriting of Gonzaga history (Molly Bourne); and whether image is everything--visual art as self-advertising in Europe and America (Larry Silver). Nelson is Coordinator of Art History at Syracuse University Abroad in Florence. Zeckhauser is Frank P. Ramsey Professor of Political Economy in the Kennedy School of Government at Harvard University. Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Philip J. Cook of Duke University reviews “The Economics of Crime: An Introduction to Rational Crime Analysis” by Harold Winter,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Undergraduate textbook presents an introduction to the economic analysis of crime. Discusses rational crime basics; efficient punishment and fines; prison and crime deterrence; the death penalty and crime deterrence; race and crime; private crime deterrence; drugs and crime; social reforms and crime deterrence; and what economists do. Winter is Associate Professor at Ohio University. Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Giuseppe Bertola of Universita di Torino reviews “The Economics of Inaction: Stochastic Control Models with Fixed Costs” by Nancy L. Stokey,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Provides an introduction to stochastic control models in economics that feature fixed adjustment costs or other elements that lead to inaction regions. Discusses stochastic processes, Brownian motions, and diffusions; stochastic integrals and Ito’s lemma; martingales; useful formulas for Brownian motions; exercising an option; models with fixed costs; models with fixed and variable costs; models with continuous control variables; regulated Brownian motion; investment--linear and convex adjustment costs; and an aggregate model with fixed costs. Stokey is Frederick Henry Prince Professor of Economics at the University of Chicago. Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Larry Samuelson of Yale University reviews “The Foundations of Positive and Normative Economics: A Handbook” by Andrew Caplin, Andrew Schotter,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Fifteen papers, resulting from a New York University conference held in August 2006, consider how best to incorporate new measurement technologies related to choice behavior into the current, united paradigm of economics. Papers discuss the case for mindless economics; the case for mindful economics; what is so informative about choice; two points of view regarding revealed preference and behavioral economics; some thoughts on the principle of revealed preference; mindless or mindful economics--a methodological evaluation; choice-theoretic foundations for behavioral welfare economics; revealed mistakes and revealed preferences; the economist as therapist--methodological ramifications of “light” paternalism; look-ups as the windows of the strategic soul; revealed preference and bounded rationality; the seven properties of good models; researcher incentives and empirical methods; choice and process--theory ahead of measurement; and economic theory and psychological data--bridging the divide. Caplin is Professor of Economics and Codirector of the Center for Experimental Social Science at New York University. Schotter is Professor of Economics and Director of the Center for Experimental Social Science at New York University. Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Roger D. Congleton of George Mason University reviews “Free Riding” by Richard Tuck,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Examines the possibility that the phenomenon of free riding, or declining to contribute to a collective project if the contribution is negligible, is a recent, historically contingent concept. Discusses the prisoners’ dilemma; voting and other thresholds; negligibility; rule and act utilitarianism; and perfect competition, oligopoly, and monopoly. Tuck is Frank G. Thomson Professor of Government at Harvard University. Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Rod Falvey of University of Nottingham reviews “Measuring Globalisation: Gauging Its Consequences” by Axel Dreher, Noel Gaston, Pim Martens,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Presents a framework for defining globalization and analyzing the relationships among economic, political, and social variables. Discusses the move toward an understanding of the concept of globalization; the measurement of globalization; and consequences of globalization reconsidered--applying the KOF Index. Dreher is at the KOF Swiss Economic Institute at ETH Zurich. Gaston is at Bond University. Martens is at Maastricht University. Author and subject indexes.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: John Whalley of University of Western Ontario and Centre for International Governance Innovation reviews “The Impacts of 9/11 on Canada-U.S. Trade” by Steven Globerman, Paul Storer,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Presents a statistical analysis of trade flows between the United States and Canada since 9/11 and considers the quantitative effects of recent border entry security initiatives on bilateral trade flows. Discusses security policy and the Canada-U.S. border; an overview of Canada-U.S. trade in goods; the impacts of border security--a review of the literature; the study methodology; the aggregate export and import equations; estimating export and import equations at the port level; interpreting the estimated impacts at individual ports; and potential impacts on capital investment. Globerman is Kaiser Professor of International Business, and Storer is Associate Professor in the College of Business and Economics, at Western Washington University. Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Alan V. Deardorff of University of Michigan reviews “Blue-Collar Blues: Is Trade to Blame for Rising US Income Inequality?” by Robert Z. Lawrence,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Explores the links between slow U.S. real wage growth, increased earnings inequality, and trade. Discusses the wage-productivity gap, 1981-2006; wage inequality and trade; class inequality and trade; globalization, stock options, and the super rich; and job dislocation--past and future. Lawrence is a nonresident Senior Fellow at the Peterson Institute and Albert L. Williams Professor of Trade and Investment in the John F. Kennedy School of Government at Harvard University. Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Robert H. Frank of Cornell University reviews “Crunch: Why Do I Feel So Squeezed? (And Other Unsolved Economic Mysteries)” by Jared Bernstein,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Presents easy-to-understand answers to questions working Americans want to ask economists. Discusses why people feel economically squeezed; gross domestic product; political economy; globalization; and the reconnection agenda. Bernstein is Senior Economist and Director of the Living Standards Program at the Economic Policy Institute. Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Mark A. Carlson of Federal Reserve Board reviews “The Evolution of Monetary Policy and Banking in the US” by Donald D. Hester,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Analyzes the evolution of monetary policy and banking institutions in the United States over the past sixty years, focusing on the dynamic interactions between the Federal Reserve and banking institutions that resulted from financial market innovations. Discusses Marriner S. Eccles and Thomas B. McCabe, 1945-51; William McChesney Martin, Jr., 1951-70; Arthur F. Burns and G. William Miller, 1970-79; Paul A. Volcker, 1979-87; Alan Greenspan, 1987-2006; Benjamin S. Bernanke, 2006-the present; an overview and summary of the Federal Reserve and monetary policy; the first twenty-five years after World War II; resolution--1971-2007; and an overview and summary of recovery, growth, and adaptation in U.S. banking. Hester is Professor of Economics, Emeritus at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. No index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Jordi Gali of CREI and Universitat Pompeu Fabra reviews “Monetary Policy Strategy” by Frederic S. Mishkin,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Eighteen papers, some previously published, present Frederic S. Mishkin’s work on the changes in the conduct of monetary policy in recent years, focusing on the turn to inflation targeting. Papers discuss what central banks should do; the transmission mechanism and the role of asset prices in monetary policy; the role of output stabilization in the conduct of monetary policy; whether central bank transparency can go too far; whether there is a role for monetary aggregates in the conduct of monetary policy; rethinking the role of the nonaccelerating inflation rate of unemployment in monetary policy--implications of model formulation and uncertainty; central bank behavior and the strategy of monetary policy--observations from six industrialized countries; whether inflation targeting is a new framework for monetary policy; international experiences with different monetary policy regimes; why the Federal Reserve should adopt inflation targeting; inflation targeting in emerging market countries; monetary policy strategies for Latin America; monetary policy strategies for emerging market countries--lessons from Latin America; inflation targeting in transition economies--experience and prospects; a decade of inflation targeting in the world--what we know and what we need to know; the dangers of exchange-rate pegging in emerging market countries; the mirage of exchange-rate regimes for emerging market countries;… Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Charles Wyplosz of Graduate Institute, Geneva reviews “Regional Monetary Integration” by Peter B. Kenen, Ellen E. Meade,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Surveys the prospects for regional monetary integration in various parts of the world, focusing on the structure and functioning of the European Monetary Union, North America, South America, and East Asia. Discusses the forms, costs, and benefits of currency consolidation; the European Monetary Union; monetary arrangements and economic performance; monetary union in the Americas; monetary union in East Asia; and the outlook and implications for the United States. Kenen is Adjunct Senior Fellow for International Economics with the Council on Foreign Relations and Walker Professor of Economics and Finance, Emeritus, at Princeton University. Meade is Associate Professor in the Department of Economics at American University. Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Uday Rajan of University of Michigan reviews “Pop Finance: Investment Clubs and the New Investor Populism” by Brooke Harrington,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Follows the trajectory of the new stock market populism via the rise of investment clubs throughout the 1990s, through which millions of people across the socioeconomic spectrum became investors for the first time. Discusses stock market populism--investment clubs and economic history; investment clubs as markets in microcosm; group composition and the business case for diversity; getting ahead versus getting along--decision making in investment clubs; and reflections on investing in the 1990s. Harrington is a researcher at the Max Planck Institute for the Study of Societies. Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Philipppe Jorion of University of California at Irvine reviews “Plight of the Fortune Tellers: Why We Need to Manage Financial Risk Differently” by Riccardo Rebonato,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Explores how to revisit ideas about probability in financial risk management, focusing on the importance of decision making. Discusses thinking about risk; thinking about probabilities; making choices; what risk management is for; some of the changes that have occurred in the financial industry in the last few decades; looking beneath the surface--hidden problems; which type of probability matters in risk management; the promise of economic capital; and what we can do instead in financial risk management. Rebonato is the global head of market risk and global head of quantitative research and quantitative analysis with the Royal Bank of Scotland. Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Sudipto Bhattacharya of London School of Economics and Political Science reviews “Why Are There So Many Banking Crises? The Politics and Policy of Bank Regulation” by Jean-Charles Rochet,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Ten previously published papers examine the causes of banking crises around the world in recent decades, focusing on the effects of political interference. Papers discuss why there are so many banking crises; coordination failures and the lender of last resort--whether Walter Bagehot was right after all; the lender of last resort--a twenty-first century approach; macroeconomic shocks and banking supervision; interbank lending and systemic risk; controlling risk in payment systems; systemic risk, interbank relations, and the central bank; capital requirements and the behavior of commercial banks; rebalancing the three pillars of Basel II; and the three pillars of Basel II--optimizing the mix. Rochet is Professor of Mathematics and Economics at the University of Toulouse. No index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Ann-Charlotte Stahlberg of Stockholm University reviews “The Gender Impact of Social Security Reform” by Estelle James, Alejandra Cox Edwards, Rebeca Wong,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Compares the gendered outcomes of social security systems in Chile, Argentina, and Mexico, and presents empirical findings from Eastern and Central European transition economies as well as several OECD countries. Discusses why social security systems and social security reforms have a gender impact; living arrangements and standards of elderly men and women; how we measure the impact of social security systems and reforms; Chile; Argentina; Mexico; and gender issues in social security reforms of other regions; design features that determine gender outcomes. James is Professor Emeritus at the State University of New York, Stony Brook, and a consultant to the World Bank and other organizations. Edwards is Professor of Economics at California State University, Long Beach. Wong is Professor of Population Economics at the University of Texas Medical Branch/Galveston, Director of the WHO/PAHO Collaborating Center for Pan-American Aging and Health, and Research Associate at the Population Studies Center at the University of Texas at Austin. Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Robert Bifulco of Syracuse University reviews “Spin Cycle: How Research Is Used in Policy Debates: The Case of Charter Schools” by Jeffrey R. Henig,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Explores how controversies over the charter school movement illustrate the use and misuse of research in policy debates. Discusses the New York Times/AFT Charter School controversy; informed democracy--an ideal and its skeptics; how cool research gets in hot waters--privatization, school choice, and charter schools; research in the public eye--personalization, polarization, and politicization; research outside the spotlight--accumulation, convergence, and contingency; following the money--the role of funding in the politicization of education research; how research reaches the public ear--old media and new; and whether the ideal of informed democracy can be revived. Henig is Professor of Political Science and Education at Teachers College, Columbia University, and Professor of Political Science at Columbia University. Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Damon Clark of University of Florida and National Bureau of Economic Research reviews “Improving School-to-Work Transitions” by David Neumark,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Seven papers consider the successes and failures of the 1990s-era school-to-work initiatives and assess how high schools, colleges, and government can help youths make a smoother transition into stable, well-paying jobs. Papers discuss transitions to work for racial, ethnic, and immigrant groups; participation in career and technical education and school-to-work in American high schools; whether school-to-work programs help the “forgotten half”; learning by doing career academies; the National Academy Foundation’s career academies--shaping postsecondary transitions; labor-market linkages among two-year college faculty and their impact on student perceptions, effort, and college persistence; and smoothing the transition from school to work--building job skills for a local labor market. Contributors include economists. Neumark is Professor of Economics at the University of California at Irvine and Senior Fellow at the Public Policy Institute of California. Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Marvin Krislov of Oberlin College reviews “Color and Money: How Rich White Kids Are Winning the War over College Affirmative Action” by Peter Schmidt,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Examines whether colleges misuse affirmative action to benefit wealthy white students and analyzes the ensuing racial tension that exists on college campuses. Discusses how money rises above merit; how the rich deny education to the poor; the origins of college affirmative action; profiting from preferences; the volatile mix on campus; affirmative action under attack; black voices fighting to be heard; the uprising of the excluded; fuzzy research to the rescue; the changing legal landscape; President Bush’s American dilemma; the establishment’s voice; the Supreme Court’s affirmation of affirmative action; and democracy’s intervention in the struggle. Schmidt is Deputy Editor of the Chronicle of Higher Education. Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Janet S. Netz of ApplEcon LLC reviews “The Economics of Intercollegiate Sports” by Randy R. Grant, John Leadley, Zenon Zygmont,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Sports economics textbook provides an introduction for undergraduate students to the college sports industry. Discusses the history of intercollegiate athletics and the NCAA; cartels in college sports; the labor market for college athletes; athletics and academics; the labor market for college coaches; the athletic department and the university; the media and intercollegiate sports; race and gender issues in intercollegiate sports; and reforming college sports. Includes end-of-chapter exercises. Grant is at Linfield College. Leadley and Zygmont are at Western Oregon University. Select bibliography; name and subject indexes.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Robert O. Keohane of Princeton University reviews “The Economic Structure of International Law” by Joel P. Trachtman,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Presents a law and economics-based theoretical perspective on the structure of the international legal system. Discusses the insights gained from transaction cost economics and property rights theory; the capacity for binding transfer of authority through customary international law; treaty; a law and economics perspective on the formation and utility of international organizations; the allocation of authority among different functional organizations; and the role of the adjudicator in international law. Trachtman is Professor of International Law in the Fletcher School at Tufts University. Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Valerie Y. Suslow of University of Michigan reviews “Global Price Fixing” by John M. Connor,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Updated and revised second edition describes and analyzes in depth the origins, operations, and impacts of global cartels in the markets for lysine, citric acid, and vitamins. Discusses the economics of price fixing; anticartel laws and enforcement; the citric acid industry; the citric acid conspiracy; economic impacts of the citric acid cartel; the world lysine industry; the lysine conspiracy; economic effects of the lysine cartel; the global vitamins industries; the vitamins conspiracies; effects of the vitamins cartels; U.S. government prosecutions; antitrust prosecutions outside the United States; the civil suits; the business of fighting cartels; and global price fixing--summing up. Connor is at Purdue University. Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Mine Zeynep Senses of Johns Hopkins University reviews “Job Creation and Poverty Reduction in India: Towards Rapid and Sustained Growth” by Sadiq Ahmed,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Eight papers examine growth and employment issues in India. Papers discuss India’s long-term growth experience--lessons and prospects (Sadiq Ahmed); fiscal policy for growth in India (Brian Pinto, Farah Zahir, and Gaobo Pang); India’s state finances (Marina Wes); the move from inhibiting to enabling--India’s changing approach to the role of private sector (Deepak K. Mishra); India’s financial sector--recent reforms and the challenges ahead (Priya Basu); meeting India’s infrastructure demands--the role of reforms and investment (Clive Harris); revitalizing the agricultural sector in India--opportunities and challenges (Dina Umali-Deininger); and labor markets in India--developments and challenges (Ahmad Ahsan and Ashish Narain). Ahmed is Sector Director of the Poverty Reduction and Economic Management Unit of the World Bank. Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Rema Hanna of Harvard University reviews “When Things Fell Apart: State Failure in Late-Century Africa” by Robert H. Bates,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Examines late-twentieth-century state failure in Africa, focusing on Rwanda, Sudan, Liberia, and Congo. Discusses the move from fable to fact; political legacies; policy choices; subnational tensions; and when things fall apart. Bates is Eaton Professor of the Science of Government, a Faculty Fellow of the Institute for International Development, and a member of the Department of African and African-American Studies at Harvard University. Bibliography; index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Juan Carlos Hallak of Universidad de San Andres reviews “The Decline of Latin American Economies: Growth, Institutions, and Crises” by Sebastian Edwards, Gerardo Esquivel, Graciela Marquez,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Ten papers, originally presented at the NBER’s Inter-American Seminar on Economics held in Mexico City in December 2004, examine the puzzle of Latin America’s poor economic performance and consider the roles of institutions and political considerations. Papers discuss when Latin America fell behind (Leandro Prados de la Escosura); before the Golden Age--economic growth in Mexico and Portugal, 1910-50 (Pedro Lains); inequality and the evolution of institutions of taxation--evidence from the economic history of the Americas (Kenneth L. Sokoloff and Eric M. Zolt); financial crises, 1880-1913--the role of foreign currency debt (Michael D. Bordo and Christopher M. Meissner); the true measure of country risk--a primer on the interrelations between solvency and the polity structure of emerging markets, Argentina 1886-92 (Gerardo della Paolera and Martin Grandes); related lending--manifest looting or good governance?--lessons from the economic history of Mexico (Noel Maurer and Stephen Haber); sudden stops and currency drops--a historical look (Luis A. V. Catao); establishing credibility--the role of foreign advisors in Chile’s 1955-58 stabilization program (Sebastian Edwards); some economic effects of closing the economy--the Mexican experience in the mid-twentieth century (Gerardo Esquivel and Graciela Marquez); and the political economy of protectionism--the Mexican textile industry, 1900-1950 (Aurora Gomez-Galvarriato). Edwards is Henry Ford II… Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Paul Glewwe of University of Minnesota reviews “Land in Transition: Reform and Poverty in Rural Vietnam” by Martin Ravallion, Dominique van de Walle,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Presents a case study of Vietnam’s efforts to fight poverty using market-oriented land reforms. Discusses the historical context and policy debates; data and summary statistics; welfare impacts of privatizing land-use rights; land reallocation after the introduction of a land market; whether rising landlessness is a sign of success or failure; and access to credit for the landless poor. Ravallion is Director of the Development Research Group at the World Bank. Van de Walle is Lead Economist in the Gender and Development Group at the World Bank. Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Barry R. Chiswick of University of Illinois at Chicago and IZA - Institute for the Study of Labor reviews “The Marketplace of Christianity” by Robert B. Ekelund, Robert F. Hebert, Robert D. Tollison,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Applies the tools of economic theory to illuminate the emergence of Protestantism in the sixteenth century and to examine contemporary religion-influenced issues, including evolution and gay marriage. Discusses religion, church, and economics; the economics of religion; religious markets; religious form change--case studies; economics of the Protestant revolt; the Counter-Reformation--incumbent-firm reaction to market entry; the establishment and evolution of Protestantism; Catholicism, Protestantism, and economic performance; and the competitive revolution in Christianity. Ekelund is Professor of Economics and Edward K. and Catherine L. Lowder Eminent Scholar Emeritus, and Hebert is Russell Foundation Professor Emeritus, at Auburn University. Tollison is Professor of Economics and BB&T Senior Fellow at Clemson University. Glossary; index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Arjo Klamer of Erasmus University reviews “Measuring the Value of Culture: Methods and Examples in Cultural Economics” by Jeanette D. Snowball,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Provides a practical guide to conducting valuation studies of culture and cultural goods, and a means of interpreting the results for potential funders. Discusses the arts, economics, and valuation; using economic impact studies to value the arts; calculating economic impact; the contingent valuation method; using willingness to pay studies to value cultural goods; and the choice experiment method and use. Snowball is in the Department of Economics at Rhodes University. Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Thomas C. Leonard of Princeton University reviews “The Dismal Science: How Thinking Like an Economist Undermines Community” by Stephan A. Marglin,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Explores the ways in which the foundational assumptions of economics may undermine a sense of community and justify a world in which individuals are isolated and impoverished in terms of social connections. Discusses economics, the market, and community; what community is and whether it is worth the cost; the cutting edge of modernity; individualism; some history; the move form vice to virtue in a century; how we know when we do not know; sources of the modern ideology of knowledge; taking experience seriously; welfare economics and the nation-state; why enough is never enough; the economics of tragic choices; and the move from imperialism to globalization, by way of development. Marglin is Walter S. Barker Professor of Economics at Harvard University. Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Emily Oster of University of Chicago reviews “EconoPower: How a New Generation of Economists Is Transforming the World” by Mark Skousen,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Examines how economics has gained an increased influence over the other branches of social science and how economists are solving the world’s problems on both individual and national levels. Focuses on personal finance--earning, saving, investing, and retiring; economists entering the corporate boardroom; solving domestic problems; solving international problems; and predicting the future. Skousen is Benjamin Franklin Chair of Management at Grantham University. Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Kevin D. Hoover of Duke University reviews “Hunting Causes and Using Them: Approaches in Philosophy and Economics” by Nancy Cartwright,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Provides a critical survey of the philosophical and economic literature on causality, with a special focus on Bayes-nets and invariance methods. Discusses causation--one word, many things; causal claims--warranting them and using them; where the theory is in our “theories” of causality; what is wrong with Bayes nets; whether modularity fails; comments against modularity, the causal Markov condition, and any link between the two; the move from metaphysics to method--comments on manipulability and the causal Markov condition; two theorems on invariance and causality; probabilities and experiments; how to get causes from probabilities; the merger of cause and strategy; the vanity of rigor in economics--theoretical models and Galilean experiments; and counterfactuals in economics--a commentary. Cartwright is Professor of Philosophy at the London School of Economics and Political Science and at the University of California, San Diego, and is Fellow of the British Academy. Bibliography; index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Anna Jacobson Schwartz of National Bureau of Economic Research reviews “Milton Friedman: A Biography” by Lanny Ebenstein,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Traces the life of Milton Friedman and examines his continuing relevance to our political and economic circumstances. Discusses his early life; his undergraduate years; the University of Chicago and Columbia; Rose; World War II; the return to academe; the Department of Economics at the University of Chicago; “Positive Economics”; family; professorship; <I>A Theory of the Consumption Function; John Maynard Keynes; A Monetary History of the United States; the Chicago school of economics; Capitalism and Freedom; travel and Goldwater; colleagues; public intellectual and policy proposals; Richard Nixon and the Nobel Prize; Free to Choose; Ronald Reagan and international influence; Friedrich Hayek and the role of ideas; school vouchers and social issues; and the Friedman Prize. Bibliographical essay; index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: W. Max Corden of University of Melbourne reviews “Harry Johnson: A Life in Economics” by Donald E. Moggridge,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Chronicles the intellectual development of economist Harry Johnson and considers his contributions to economics, economic education, and the discussion of economic policy, especially in Canada and Great Britain. Discusses Johnson’s origins in Toronto; his early career in Antigonish, Nova Scotia; his military experience in England; North American postgraduate work; his experience at Cambridge; his role as a Cambridge economist; working in Manchester; his move to Chicago; Canada, economic nationalism, and opulence, 1957-66; Chicago--money, trade, and development; the London School of Economics; professional life--largely British; money and inflation; the International Monetary System; Johnson’s “Wicksell Period”; and Johnson’s stroke and the aftermath. Moggridge is Professor of Economics at the University of Toronto. Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Lauren E. Feiler of Carleton College reviews “Augustin Cournot: Modelling Economics” by Jean-Philippe Touffut,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Seven papers, originally presented at a conference held at the Cournot Centre for Economic Studies in December 2005, examine the pioneering work of Antoine Augustin Cournot in the fields of economics, game theory, sociology, and epistemology of probability and statistics. Papers discuss Cournot as economist--two hundred years of relevance (Jean Magnan de Bornier); Cournot’s probabilistic epistemology (Thierry Martin); the functions of economic models (Bernard Walliser); the move from Cournot’s principle to market efficiency (Glenn Shafer); war and peace (Robert J. Aumann); Cournot and the social income (Robert M. Solow); and comparing the incomparable--the sociology of statistics (Alain Desrosieres). Touffut is Director of the Cournot Centre for Economic Studies. Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Saul H. Hymans of University of Michigan reviews “The Cult of Statistical Significance: How the Standard Error Costs Us Jobs, Justice, and Lives” by Stephen T. Ziliak, Deirdre N. McCloskey,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Examines the flaws in the scientific technique of “statistical significance” through an exploration of its application in a broad spectrum of fields, and considers how to bring the statistical sciences back on track. Discusses statistical significance as a significant problem; dieting “significance” and the case of Vioxx; the sizeless stare of statistical significance; what the sizeless scientists say in defense; better practice---beta-importance versus alpha-“significance”; what can go wrong in the use of significance tests in economics; what went wrong in the American Economic Review during the 1980s; whether economic practice is improving; how big is big in economics; what the sizeless stare costs, economically speaking; how economics stays that way--the textbooks and the referees; the not-boring rise of significance in psychology; whether psychometrics lacks power; the psychology of psychological significance testing; medicine seeking a magic pill; Kenneth Rothman’s revolt; drugs, disability, and death; Francis Edgeworth’s significance; Karl Pearson’s rule; statistical significance in Pearson’s journal Biometrika; William Sealy Gosset--the fable of the bee; R. A. Fisher--the fable of the wasp; how the wasp stung the bee and took over some sciences; eighty years of trained incapacity--how such a thing could happen; and what to do. Ziliak is Professor of Economics at… Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Francisco Rodriguez of United Nations Development Programme and Wesleyan University reviews “A Year without “Made in China”: One Family\'s True Life Adventure in the Global Economy” by Sara Bongiorni,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Chronicles the story of one family that embarked on a yearlong boycott of Chinese products in order to determine whether they could live without the world's fastest growing economy. Discusses excluding Chinese products from the author's home; the difficulty of finding non-Chinese children's shoes and toys; the difficulties that arose during the boycott; China's relationship with Wal-Mart; China's influence in France and in the electronics market; the difficulty of finding clothing not made in China; the family's growing acceptance of the boycott and the difficulty of finding non-Chinese office supplies; Hurricane Katrina and questions about the ethics of a boycott in a time of personal tragedy; considering whether to extend the boycott past one year; Christmas shopping and the boycott; and the end of the boycott. Bongiorni is an author and former business reporter. Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Taryn Dinkelman of Princeton University reviews “Annual World Bank Conference on Development Economics--Global 2007: Rethinking Infrastructure for Development” by Francois Bourguignon, Boris Pleskovic,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Six papers and eight comments, originally presented at the Annual World Bank Conference on Development Economics held in Tokyo in May 2006, examine the role of infrastructure in development. Papers discuss infrastructure and development--a survey of recent and upcoming issues (Antonio Estache); climate change impacts, energy, and development (Michael Grubb); managing China's energy resources (Jiang Kejun); rural infrastructure and agricultural development (Per Pinstrup-Andersen and Satoru Shimokawa); spurring economic development by capitalizing on brand agriculture--turning development strategy on its head (Masahisa Fujita); and infrastructure and regional cooperation (Haruhiko Kuroda, Masahiro Kawai, and Rita Nangia). Also includes the welcome, opening, and keynote addresses presented at the conference. Bourguignon is Chief Economist and Senior Vice President of the World Bank. Pleskovic is Research Manager in Development Economics at the World Bank. No index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Jordan Matsudaira of Cornell University reviews “The Price of Independence: The Economics of Early Adulthood” by Sheldon Danziger, Cecilia Elena Rouse,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Ten papers examine how economic conditions affect young people's transition to adulthood, focusing on the lengthening and increasingly varied transitions in recent generations. Papers discuss failure to launch--crossnational trends in the transition to economic independence; whether the company man is an anachronism--trends in long-term employment in the United States, 1973-2006; health insurance and the transition to adulthood; blurring the boundary--changes in collegiate participation and the transition to adulthood; labor market experiences and transitions to adulthood; young adults leaving the nest--the role of the cost of living; sticking around--delayed departure from the parental nest in Western Europe; to have and to hold--an analysis of young adult debt; family background and children's transitions to adulthood over time; and early incarceration spells and the transition to adulthood. Danziger is Henry J. Meyer Distinguished University Professor of Public Policy and Codirector of the National Poverty Center in the Gerald R. Ford School of Public Policy at the University of Michigan. Rouse is Theodore A. Wells '29 Professor of Economics and Public Affairs at Princeton University and Director of the Princeton Education Research Section. Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Richard Green of University of Birmingham reviews “Electricity and Energy Policy in Britain, France and the United States since 1945” by Martin Chick, Martin Chick,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Presents a major economic and historical study of the development of electricity and energy policy in Britain, France, and the United States since 1945. Discusses shifting from coal to oil--what price security?; the European Coal and Steel Community; moving the margin to the center--pricing electricity; electricity investment--rewarding the past, discounting the future; and deregulation, privatization, and liberalization. Chick is Senior Lecturer in Economic and Social History at the University of Edinburgh. Bibliography; index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Stefan Szymanski of City University London reviews “Economics, Uncertainty and European Football: Trends in Competitive Balance” by Loek Groot,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Explores the development of competitive balance in the major European football countries over an extended period of time and considers some policy prescriptions for the governance of the European football market. Discusses using football statistics--the basic techniques; competitive balance--sport's most precious good; static competitive balance; competitive balance based on team quality; dynamic competitive balance; and the future of European football--back to the 1950s. Groot is Associate Professor of Public Sector Economics in the Utrecht School of Economics at Utrecht University. Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Catherine D. Wolfram of University of California, Berkeley reviews “The Unsustainable Costs of Partial Deregulation” by Paul W. MacAvoy,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Assesses the results of deregulation in the United States over the last thirty years and analyzes whether deregulation has achieved any of its stated goals in the electricity, gas delivery, and telecommunications industries. Discusses an introduction to network technology and market structure; the regulation of networks; electric and gas network performance and partial deregulation; the strategic response of Pacific Gas and Electric Corporation to partial deregulation during the California power crisis; the long distance telephone networks and partial deregulation; and the singular result of partial deregulation and what can be done. MacAvoy is Williams Brothers Professor Emeritus of Management Studies at Yale University. Bibliography; index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: John T. Cuddington of Colorado School of Mines reviews “A Handbook of Primary Commodities in the Global Economy” by Marian Radetzki,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Examines the increasingly crucial role of commodities in the world economy and considers pertinent issues surrounding international commodity markets. Discusses the historical framework; the geography of commodity production and trade; comparative advantage and trade policy distortions; price formation and price trends in commodities; the commodity exchanges, commodity investments, and speculation; the economics of exhaustible resource depletion; fears of, and measures to assure, supply security; producer cartels in international commodity markets; public ownership in primary commodity production; and the monoeconomies--issues raised by heavy dependence on commodity production and exports. Radetzki is Professor of Economics at Lulea University of Technology. Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Neviana Petkova of University of Oregon reviews “Trade Liberalisation: Impact on Growth and Trade in Developing Countries” by Ashok Parikh,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Nine papers, most previously published, present a quantitative assessment of trade liberalization and its impact on micro and macro economics structure in developing countries. Papers discuss disciplining firms--the impact of trade reforms on profit margins in the Indian industry (Uma S. Kambhampati and Ashok Parikh); whether liberalization has affected profit margins in the Indian industry (Kambhampati and Parikh); exports, inward foreign direct investment, and regional economic growth in China (Haishun Sun and Parikh); the impact of trade liberalization on import demands in India--a panel data analysis for commodity groups (Rajesh Mehta and Parikh); whether trade liberalization accelerates convergence in per capita incomes in developing countries (Parikh and Miyuki Shibata); dynamics of the relationship between the terms of trade and the trade balance in developing countries of Asia, Africa, and Latin America (Parikh and Shibata); the relationship between trade liberalization, economic growth, and balance of payments in developing countries (Parikh and Corneliu Stirbu); the relationship between trade liberalization, growth, and balance of payments in developing countries--an econometric study (Parikh); and instability and volatility of capital flows in developing countries (Alberto Gabriele, Korkut Boratav, and Parikh). Parikh is in the Department of Economics at the University of East Anglia. Author and subject… Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Stephen Devereux of Institute of Development Studies, University of Sussex reviews “Famine in North Korea: Markets, Aid, and Reform” by Stephan Haggard, Marcus Noland,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Presents an account of the late twentieth-century North Korean famine, focusing on the origins and aftermath of the crisis, the regime's response to outside aid, and the effect of its current policies on the country's economic future. Discusses famine, aid, and markets in North Korea; the origins of the great famine; the distribution of misery--famine and the breakdown of the public distribution system; the aid regime--the problem of monitoring; diversion; the political economy of aid; coping, marketization, and reform--new sources of vulnerability; and North Korea in comparative and international perspective. Haggard is Lawrence and Sallye Krause Professor in the Graduate School of International Relations and Pacific Studies at the University of California, San Diego. Noland is Senior Fellow at the Institute for International Economics. Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Edward N. Wolff of New York University reviews “The Warhol Economy: How Fashion, Art, and Music Drive New York City” by Elizabeth Currid,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Examines how creative industries--fashion, art, and music--drive the economy of New York City. Discusses art, culture, and New York City; how it all began--the move from the rise of the factory to the rise of bling; becoming creative; the social life of creativity; the economics of a dance floor; creating buzz and selling cool; and the rise of global tastemakers--what it all means for the policymakers. Currid is Assistant Professor in the University of Southern California's School of Policy, Planning, and Development. Index.”

title: Book Reviews
abstract: Robert E. Wright of New York University reviews “Political Institutions and Financial Development” by Stephen Haber, Douglass C. North, Barry R. Weingast,. The EconLit Abstract of the reviewed work begins “Nine papers examine why some countries develop better financial systems than others, focusing on the importance of a country's political institutions in this development. Papers discuss political institutions and financial development--evidence from the political economy of bank regulation in Mexico and the United States (Stephen Haber); the political economy of early U.S. financial development (Richard Sylla); what the World Bank can learn from American history (John Joseph Wallis); the move beyond legal origin and checks and balances--political credibility, citizen information, and financial sector development (Philip Keefer); the microeconomic effects of different approaches to bank supervision (James R. Barth, Gerard Caprio, and Ross Levine); political drivers of diverging corporate governance patterns (Peter Gourevitch and James Shinn); credible commitment and sovereign default risk--two bond markets and imperial Brazil (William R.
